title: Short-Term Reversal Persists Globally -- If Properly Measured
data_sample: Monthly stock-level panel, 64 developed and emerging countries, January 1990 to December 2023. US data from CRSP, international from Compustat, all returns in USD. Filters: common stocks on main exchanges only; excludes missing returns, price <= $1, missing industry code, nano-caps; requires >=10 stocks per country-month. Sample: 7,206-21,698 stocks/month, avg 14,193, 5,790,595 total stock-month observations.

signals.name: Industry-adjusted reversal
signals.definition: REV_IN = R_{i,t-1} - mean(R_{j,t-1}) across a stock's industry peers, i.e. a stock's prior-month return minus its industry peers' average prior-month return.

signals.name: Regret-based reversal
signals.definition: REG = R_{i,t-1} - max(R_{k,t-1} for k in the same industry), deviation from the best-performing peer in the industry (Arisoy et al. 2024). Per the paper's own spanning regression, subsumed by industry-adjusted reversal and not independently useful.

portfolio_construction: Within each country and month, sort stocks into quintiles by signal. Long the bottom quintile (worst relative performers), short the top quintile (best relative performers). Both equal- and value-weighted variants computed; headline/Table 1-3 results use value-weighted. Monthly rebalance, no formation/holding lag subtlety beyond the standard one-month reversal window.

key_results.label: United States
key_results.significance: t=1.38, spanning alpha vs industry-adjusted=0.15 (t=0.63, insignificant)

central_claim: Short-term reversal appears to have weakened in modern, liquid markets, but this is a measurement artifact: raw return signals mix a firm-specific component (which reverses) with an industry-wide component (which persists). Stripping out the industry component via an industry-adjusted signal restores a large, statistically significant reversal effect across international equity markets, including large developed markets like the US, UK, and Japan.
testability_notes: Sample runs through Dec 2023, which overlaps Alpaca's 2016+ coverage for the tail of the paper's own 'second subperiod' (2007-2023) -- unlike paper #2, whose sample ends entirely before 2016. Only the US row is realistically testable with Alpaca (US equities only); the industry-adjusted signal additionally requires an industry classification Alpaca doesn't provide (resolved separately via SEC EDGAR + Fama-French 12, see papers/paper-01-ssrn-6630998/reproduce/). The US result is the paper's weakest major-market result (t=2.12 vs UK 5.37, Japan 4.63), so a genuine replication attempt should not expect UK/Japan-level significance. The regret-based signal doesn't need separate testing since the paper's own spanning regression shows it's subsumed by industry-adjusted reversal.
open_questions: The paper doesn't specify its industry taxonomy (likely GICS or a Compustat/CRSP-standard scheme) -- we substitute Fama-French 12, a standard but different classification.
Whether the industry peer mean includes or excludes the stock itself ('peers' is ambiguous) -- we assume exclusion (leave-one-out).
No US-only subperiod breakdown is reported in the main tables, only global pooled -- we can't check whether the US-specific effect has weakened over time within the paper's own results.
